Right to Be Forgotten on Facebook, Instagram and Social Networks

By RMA — Web Reputation Agency

The right to be forgotten on Facebook works differently depending on who published the content. Your own posts, photos and account can be deleted with Meta's built-in tools, content others posted about you requires a report or a formal GDPR request, and a deceased person's profile can be memorialised or removed by family. In every case, the legal basis for people in Italy is the GDPR right of erasure under Article 17, applied to Meta Platforms Ireland as data controller.

Your own content: deleting posts, photos and accounts

Anything you published yourself can be removed without asking anyone, and this is the fastest form of erasure available on any social network. On Facebook and Instagram the Activity Log and "Your activity" sections let you filter posts, comments, likes and tags by date and delete them in bulk.

Before deleting an entire account, download a copy of your information from the Accounts Centre, because deletion is irreversible once the grace period ends. Meta distinguishes between deactivation, which hides the profile but keeps everything, and permanent deletion, which you can cancel only during the first thirty days. After that, Meta states that removing data from its systems can take up to ninety days, while some copies may remain in backups or be retained for legal obligations. Messages you sent to others usually stay in their inboxes, which surprises many users.

On LinkedIn, X and TikTok the logic is similar: delete individual posts or close the account through the settings, and check the option that controls whether search engines may show your public profile. Turning this off on Facebook and LinkedIn is an effective first step when the goal is to reduce what appears in Google under your name.

Content others posted about you

When someone else published a photo, a post or a comment about you, the first step is a direct request to that person, followed by a report to the platform if they refuse. Many conflicts in Italian families, schools and workplaces end at this stage, simply because the author did not realise the content caused harm.

Platform reporting routes

Facebook and Instagram offer specific forms for privacy violations, which are separate from the generic "report post" button. In the EU, a person can ask Meta to remove an image or video in which they are identifiable when it violates their privacy, and stronger protection applies to minors, intimate images and content revealing addresses or identity documents. Tags can be removed by you at any time, and you can require approval before tags appear on your profile.

  • Use the privacy violation form for images and videos of you, attaching the URL and explaining your relationship to the content.
  • Use the impersonation report for fake profiles using your name or photos.
  • Use the illegal content notice for defamatory or threatening posts, citing the relevant Italian rule, such as art. 595 c.p. on defamation.

The Digital Services Act

Under the Digital Services Act, platforms must process notices of illegal content diligently, inform you of their decision with reasons and offer an internal complaint system, as well as access to certified out-of-court dispute settlement bodies. These obligations do not change what counts as illegal, but they make silence or unexplained refusals harder to justify; our article on platform liability after the Digital Services Act explains the mechanism in detail.

Filing a GDPR erasure request with Meta

When reports through the standard tools fail, a formal request under the GDPR right of erasure obliges Meta to answer within one month, extendable by two months in complex cases. For users in the EU, the controller is Meta Platforms Ireland Limited, and requests can be sent through the dedicated privacy contact forms in the Help Centre, which include a channel to the Data Protection Officer.

A strong request identifies the exact URLs, explains which personal data concern you, and states the ground under Article 17: the data are no longer necessary, you withdraw consent, you object to the processing and there are no overriding legitimate grounds, or the processing is unlawful. Attach evidence, such as previous reports and their outcomes, and keep a copy of everything you send. The right to erasure on social media is not absolute: content of genuine public interest, journalism and the exercise of freedom of expression by others can prevail, and Meta will rely on that balance when it refuses.

A report asks Meta to apply its own rules; a GDPR request asks it to comply with the law. When the first fails, the second creates a formal record that authorities can review.

The account of a deceased person

Close family members or the executor can ask Facebook and Instagram to memorialise or remove the profile of a person who has died. A memorialised account stays visible with the word "Remembering" next to the name, while removal deletes it entirely; both requests require proof of death and, for removal, proof of the relationship or authority.

Italian law adds an important rule. Art. 2-terdecies of the Codice Privacy allows the rights over a deceased person's data to be exercised by someone with their own interest, by someone acting on behalf of the deceased, or for family reasons worthy of protection, unless the deceased expressly prohibited it in writing. This provision is useful when a family in Rome or Bologna needs to remove sensitive posts or obtain access to data that the platform's own procedure does not cover. Users can also appoint a legacy contact in their settings, which avoids disputes later.

Removing social content from Google results

Deleting a post on a social network does not instantly remove it from Google, which may keep a cached title and snippet until it recrawls the page. Once the content is gone or the profile is set to private, the Search Console Outdated Content tool lets anyone ask Google to refresh the result.

If the post remains online because the platform refused, a right to be forgotten request to Google is a separate route, with its own balancing test described in our overview of what Google can really remove. Viral videos copied across several accounts and platforms need a coordinated approach, outlined in our guide to negative videos on YouTube, TikTok and Reels.

When to escalate to the Garante

If Meta or another social network ignores or rejects a well-founded erasure request, you can file a complaint with the Garante per la protezione dei dati personali in Italy. Because Meta's European headquarters are in Ireland, the Irish Data Protection Commission acts as lead authority, but the Garante receives and handles complaints from Italian residents through the GDPR cooperation mechanism.

A complaint is far more effective when it arrives with a complete dossier, prepared in this order:

  1. dated screenshots and the exact URLs of the content;
  2. copies of every report and erasure request, with the dates they were sent;
  3. Meta's replies, or proof that the one-month deadline passed without an answer;
  4. a short statement of the harm the content is causing you.

Where the content is also a criminal matter, such as defamation, threats or the non-consensual sharing of intimate images, a report to the Polizia Postale should run in parallel.
